answer:
Assume the transit is central, so the planet’s centre moves along a stellar diameter. Let

\[
D_* = 1.40\times 10^6\ \mathrm{km},\qquad
D_p = 0.10D_* = 1.40\times 10^5\ \mathrm{km}.
\]

The observed duration is \(T=6.0\ \mathrm{h}\).

### 1. Duration = first to last contact
First contact is when the planet’s leading limb first touches the star’s limb. Last contact is when the planet’s trailing limb finally leaves the opposite limb. Along the central chord, the planet’s centre travels

\[
L_{1\to4}=D_*+D_p.
\]

This is because, at the two exterior tangencies, the separation of the centres is \(R_*+R_p\) on each side, so the total distance is \(2(R_*+R_p)=D_*+D_p\).

\[
L=1.40\times10^6+1.40\times10^5
=1.54\times10^6\ \mathrm{km}.
\]

Thus

\[
v=\frac{L}{T}
=\frac{1.54\times10^6\ \mathrm{km}}{6.0\ \mathrm{h}}
=2.57\times10^5\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}
\approx 71\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}.
\]

### 2. Duration = second to third contact
Second contact is when the planet is just fully inside the stellar disc; third contact is when it is just about to begin leaving. Along a central chord the planet’s centre travels

\[
L_{2\to3}=D_*-D_p.
\]

The centre moves from \(-(R_*-R_p)\) to \(+(R_*-R_p)\), a distance \(2(R_*-R_p)=D_*-D_p\).

\[
L=1.40\times10^6-1.40\times10^5
=1.26\times10^6\ \mathrm{km}.
\]

Therefore

\[
v=\frac{1.26\times10^6\ \mathrm{km}}{6.0\ \mathrm{h}}
=2.10\times10^5\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}
\approx 58\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}.
\]

So, if the 6.0 h duration is:

- **first-to-last contact:**  
  \[
  \boxed{v \approx 7.1\times10^4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \approx 71\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}}
  \]
  using travel distance \(D_*+D_p\).

- **second-to-third contact:**  
  \[
  \boxed{v \approx 5.8\times10^4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \approx 58\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}}
  \]
  using travel distance \(D_*-D_p\).

The difference arises because the first-to-last interval includes the finite size of the planet on both ingress and egress, whereas the second-to-third interval measures only the time during which the planet is fully projected inside the stellar disc.
